analysis.one_liner: Lets student borrowers wipe out student loans in bankruptcy like other debt.
analysis.headline: The bill had one sponsor and no cosponsors; it was referred to a House Judiciary subcommittee, never received a hearing or vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current bankruptcy law, student loans can be erased only if the borrower proves paying them would cause an 'undue hardship' — a standard courts apply so strictly that most borrowers never even try. This bill would delete that exception, letting student loans be discharged in bankruptcy like credit card debt or medical bills. It was introduced by one representative, never gained a cosponsor, and never got a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers whose student debt has become unpayable — including people who were misled by their schools, dropped out without earning a degree, or face permanent disability or long-term unemployment — would get the same bankruptcy relief available to other debtors. If the bill passed, lenders would have an incentive to lend more carefully and to negotiate relief before bankruptcy, since they could no longer count on debts being nearly impossible to erase.

how_it_helps.text: Removes the 'undue hardship' exception in bankruptcy law (11 U.S.C. § 523(a)(8)), so nonprofit, government, and private student loans could be discharged like other consumer debts.
Applies to cases filed on or after the date of enactment, so borrowers already in bankruptcy could benefit.

analysis.who_pays: Lenders and the federal government, which would absorb more losses when borrowers discharge loans in bankruptcy, and by extension future borrowers, who could face higher interest rates or tighter credit as lenders price in that risk.

drawbacks.text: Lenders argue that easy discharge of student loans raises borrowing costs for everyone, since unlike a house or a car there is no collateral to repossess, so lenders would charge higher rates or restrict lending to cover the added risk.
Because the federal government is the largest student lender, more discharges would add to federal deficits or be absorbed as losses in the federal loan program.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Restoring bankruptcy as a safety valve for student debt addresses a real hardship: borrowers currently face a legal standard so strict that even disabled and defrauded borrowers routinely fail to qualify. The costs — somewhat higher rates for future borrowers and more losses in the federal loan program — are real but modest relative to the benefit of giving overburdened borrowers a workable exit. The bill is a simple, one-section repeal of the exception rather than a finely tuned compromise.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the House Judiciary Committee and then to a subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Wm. Lacy Clay introduced the bill on October 18, 2019, and it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary.
On November 15, 2019, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Antitrust, Commercial, and Administrative Law.
No further action was taken; the bill received no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Student lenders, loan servicers, and the federal loan program are better off because the bill died: the near-impossibility of discharging student loans in bankruptcy remains, so lenders keep collecting on debts other borrowers could walk away from. Borrowers in financial distress gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Wm. Lacy Clay
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to make student loans dischargeable in bankruptcy.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee (Chair Jerrold Nadler)
against.role: Committee to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; after initial referral to a subcommittee on November 15, 2019, no further action was taken before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken, and the bill's single sponsor found no cosponsors from either party, so its partisan shape was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would let borrowers discharge student loans in bankruptcy, allowing lenders and servicers to collect on some debts they currently hold regardless of the borrower's ability to pay. Because today's 'undue hardship' standard makes discharge nearly impossible, the industry's current position depends on this exception remaining law.

The federal government originates the large majority of student loans, so more bankruptcy discharges would mean larger program losses. That cost is paired with relief for distressed borrowers and a market signal to lend more carefully.
